slides.title: Reversing the margin decline How Harlow gets back to a 3% operating margin by FY2028, and what to do first

paragraphs.text: Reversing the margin decline
How Harlow gets back to a 3% operating margin by FY2028, and what to do first
Board of Directors  |  February 2027
Presented by Dana Whitfield, Chief Executive Officer
Based solely on the Harlow briefing pack, which is synthetic benchmark data. Figures are in $ millions unless stated.

slides.title: Fix promotions, shrink and delivery pricing first. Wages are not the main problem, and the 3% target is reachable

paragraphs.text: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Fix promotions, shrink and delivery pricing first. Wages are not the main problem, and the 3% target is reachable
What happened

Operating margin fell from 3.37% to 1.02% in two years (operating income $47.9M → $15.3M) even though sales grew 6%. Wages explain only 0.30 of the 2.35-point fall. Gross margin (−1.02 pts: deeper promotions and higher shrink) and e-commerce fulfillment (−0.84 pts) explain ~80%.
Why the draft plan falls short

The 8% labor-hour cut and the e-commerce freeze cannot reach 3%: even if the full $14.5M sticks, margin reaches ~2.0%. If shrink responds as it did in FY2023–25, up to ~$10M leaks back, and FY2026 operating income lands at ~$20M, on the covenant line.
What we recommend

Seven levers worth ~$30M a year (promotion reset, vendor funding, targeted labor, shrink, six store exits at lease end, private label, delivery pricing) take margin to ~3.2% at FY2025 scale for ≤$17.5M one-time cost (cap $25M). Delivery is kept but priced closer to its cost.
What to do first

In the next 90 days: roll out the tested delivery fee chain-wide, drop money-losing promotions and reopen vendor funding, restore receiving and produce checks in low-labor stores, and serve notice on the six stores whose leases end by 2027. FY2026 operating income: ~$27M vs the $20M covenant.
Decisions today
Approve the plan in place of the across-the-board labor cut; approve the delivery-fee change. The other three loss-making stores return to the board for a vote in FY2027.
Source: Harlow briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data); team analysis.

slides.title: Wage inflation explains only 0.30 of the 2.35-point margin fall. Gross margin and e-commerce explain 80%

paragraphs.text: WHERE THE MARGIN WENT
Wage inflation explains only 0.30 of the 2.35-point margin fall. Gross margin and e-commerce explain 80%
Operating margin bridge, FY2023 → FY2025 (% of sales)
Impact at FY2025 sales
Why labor is small
Hourly wage incl. benefits rose 9.4% ($16.80 → $18.38).
But labor hours per $1,000 of sales fell 6.0% (7.02 → 6.60), so labor rose only from 11.8% to 12.1% of sales.
That productivity had a cost: shrink rose over the same period (page 5).

Note: each line is shown as % of sales; FY2023 sales $1,420M, FY2025 $1,503M. $ impacts are the change in % of sales multiplied by FY2025 sales.

slides.title: The gross-margin fall is fully explained by deeper promotions and higher shrink, and 38% of promotions lose money

paragraphs.text: GROSS MARGIN
The gross-margin fall is fully explained by deeper promotions and higher shrink, and 38% of promotions lose money
Gross-margin change by driver, FY2023 → FY2025 (pts of sales)
Promotions have grown without paying back
38% of FY2025 promotional events lost money even after counting the extra units they sold.
Vendors pay less of the cost: funding covered 55% of markdowns in FY2023 but only 46% in FY2025.
Price perception got worse anyway: 41% of customers call Harlow "more expensive" (33% in FY2023).
"Promotions work" measures sales, not profit: the deepest-promotion stores grew comparable sales 1.8% vs 0.2%, but that is correlation and ignores the lost margin.
The competitive threat is real but local
ValuMart has opened 11 stores in Harlow trade areas since 2023. Harlow stores within 3 miles had comparable sales of −4.2% vs +1.1% elsewhere.
So: keep promotions targeted where ValuMart competes, and cut the events that lose money everywhere else.
Promotional sales earn 14 pts less gross margin than regular-price sales; private label earns 12 pts more. Both gaps were unchanged over the period.

Note: promotion effect = +5.0 pts promotional share × 14-pt margin gap; private label = +1.5 pts share × 12-pt premium; shrink = +0.5 pts of sales. Together they equal the −1.02 pts observed.
Source: Harlow briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data); team analysis.

slides.title: Harlow has already cut hours 6% and shrink rose with them. Another 8% cut could hand back up to ~$10M

paragraphs.text: STORE LABOR
Harlow has already cut hours 6% and shrink rose with them. Another 8% cut could hand back up to ~$10M
Shrink by store labor intensity, FY2025 (% of sales)
The draft 8% cut, net of shrink ($M a year)

data: Shrink leak: +0.67 pts of sales if the FY2023–25 pattern repeats
Net, before any lost sales from longer queues or stock-outs

paragraphs.text: Reallocate hours instead of cutting them evenly
Protect fresh: produce is the #1 reason customers shop Harlow (58%). Restore rotation and receiving checks in Q1 and Q2 stores.
Trim where hours add little: Q4 stores have the most hours but shrink no lower than Q3 (2.3% vs 2.4%). A targeted ~3% net reduction there is worth ~$5.2M.
Test before scaling: track checkout waits and stock-outs, which the briefing pack flags as unknown.

Stores ranked by labor hours per $1,000 of sales. Managers in Q1 stores say produce rotation and receiving checks are skipped on busy days. Fresh-produce waste (45%) and receiving errors (20%) make up two-thirds of shrink.

Note: the leak estimate assumes shrink responds to hours as it did over FY2023–25 (hours −6.0%, shrink +0.5 pts). Not all of that rise was labor-driven (theft is 35% of shrink), so ~$10M is an upper estimate.
Source: Harlow briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data); team analysis.

slides.title: E-commerce loses ~$10M a year once delivery costs and lost store sales are counted, not the 6.1% profit reported

paragraphs.text: E-COMMERCE
E-commerce loses ~$10M a year once delivery costs and lost store sales are counted, not the 6.1% profit reported
Profit per order by type, FY2025 ($ per order)
Reported vs true e-commerce profit, FY2025
Two gaps in the team’s calculation
It leaves out third-party delivery, which costs $8.3M a year net of fees ($13.80 cost vs $3.10 fee per delivered order).
It treats every online sale as new. Customers say 70% would otherwise have been bought in a Harlow store.
The loss grows with volume: orders are up 2.9× since FY2023 and the home-delivered share rose from 45% to 58%.

Note: contribution from new sales = $96 basket × 30% genuinely new (70% would otherwise be bought in a Harlow store, per a survey of 2,300 customers) × 20¢ per new $ (finance estimate). FY2025: 1,331k orders, 58% home-delivered.
Source: Harlow briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data); team analysis.

slides.title: The tested delivery fee would cut the e-commerce loss by ~$2.2M a year and still keep delivery, as the owners want

paragraphs.text: E-COMMERCE
The tested delivery fee would cut the e-commerce loss by ~$2.2M a year and still keep delivery, as the owners want
Chain-wide impact if customers respond as they did in the test
Why act on this first
It has already been tested on real customers, needs no capital, and can be rolled out within weeks.
Customers moved to click-and-collect, which costs $7.40 per order to fulfil vs $18.10 net for a delivered order.
Delivery stays available, so the owners’ commitment is kept.
What comes next
Delivery contract (renews 2026): push back on the proposed 3% rise. Each 1% of rate is worth ~$0.1M a year.
E-commerce still loses ~$7.6M after the fee change: replace the "freeze" with a rule that volume grows only where each order covers its cost. Test further steps (e.g. basket minimums); not yet sized.

Note: test = 4 stores, 10 weeks, late FY2025: $7.99 fee and $100 free-delivery threshold (vs $4.99 / $75). Results applied to the FY2025 chain base. Lost sales are conservatively all treated as new-to-Harlow sales.
Source: Harlow briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data); team analysis.

slides.title: Exiting the six loss-making stores whose leases end by 2027 adds ~$4.4M a year with no lease-exit cost

paragraphs.text: STORE PORTFOLIO
Exiting the six loss-making stores whose leases end by 2027 adds ~$4.4M a year with no lease-exit cost
Annual benefit of exiting the nine weakest stores ($M)
Recommendation
Six stores: do not renew; exit as each lease ends. Notices go out now.

Three stores: give them a 12-month turnaround using the same promotion and shrink fixes, then bring a closure vote to the board in FY2027 if they still lose money. They are a contingency lever, not part of the base plan.
The nine stores: $118.0M sales, −$3.1M four-wall EBITDA. 25% of their sales would move to a nearby Harlow store ($29.5M at 12% contribution = $3.5M).

Note: benefit = removal of negative four-wall EBITDA + 25% of sales moving to nearby Harlow stores × 12% contribution. The split between the 6 and the 3 stores is pro rata (store-level data not in the pack).
Source: Harlow briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data); team analysis.

slides.title: Start with four moves the evidence already supports; the structural levers follow within 12 months

paragraphs.text: SEQUENCING
Start with four moves the evidence already supports; the structural levers follow within 12 months
First 90 days
Quick, tested, little or no capital
Within 12 months
Build the structural levers
By FY2028
Lock in and decide
Delivery pricing: roll out the $7.99 fee / $100 threshold chain-wide; renew the delivery contract while resisting the 3% rise
Promotions: drop the events the post-event review shows lose money; open vendor-funding talks for the next contract cycle
Labor: withdraw the 8% across-the-board cut; restore receiving and produce-rotation hours in Q1 and Q2 stores
Stores: serve non-renewal notice on the six stores whose leases end by 2027
Labor: store-level labor model; ~3% net hours reduction in high-labor stores
Shrink: theft and receiving-error controls; monthly shrink scorecard by store
Private label: extend the range and use it as the value answer to ValuMart
Stores: exit the six as leases end; 12-month turnaround plan for the other three
Three stores: closure vote at the board in FY2027 if they are still loss-making ($7.5M exit cost)
E-commerce: grow only where each order covers its cost; test basket minimums and click-and-collect incentives
Targets: private label 20.5%, shrink ≤2.3%, promotional share ~26%, margin ≥3.0%

Note: we follow the briefing pack in treating FY2026 as the first plan year and the covenant test year.
Source: Harlow briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data); team analysis.

slides.title: We ask the board for four decisions today

paragraphs.text: DECISIONS
We ask the board for four decisions today
Approve the margin plan
Target ≥3.0% operating margin by FY2028; FY2026 plan ~$27M operating income against the $20M covenant. Monthly tracking of the seven levers.
Replace the 8% across-the-board labor cut
Use a targeted reallocation instead: protect fresh and receiving hours in low-labor stores; ~3% net reduction in high-labor stores.
Approve the chain-wide delivery-fee change
$7.99 fee and $100 free-delivery threshold, as tested. Delivery stays; e-commerce grows only where orders cover their cost.
Approve a one-time budget of up to $10M, within the $25M cap
For store exits and the shrink, private-label and promotion programs. Note: the six lease-end exits need no vote; the other three return for a vote in FY2027 (+$7.5M).
Source: Harlow briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data); team analysis.

slides.title: Appendix: how the key numbers were calculated

paragraphs.text: APPENDIX
Appendix: how the key numbers were calculated
Margin bridge
Each cost line as % of sales, FY2023 vs FY2025. The −2.35 pts total = −1.02 gross margin, −0.84 e-commerce, −0.30 labor, −0.20 occupancy, 0.00 other SG&A. $ = pts × $1,503M.
Gross margin
Promotions +5.0 pts share × −14 pts = −0.70; private label +1.5 × +12 = +0.18; shrink −0.50. Sum −1.02, equal to the reported change.
Labor
E-commerce
Delivered orders 772k (58% of 1,331k). Fulfillment = $7.40 × 1,331k + $13.80 × 772k − $3.10 × 772k = $18.1M (matches P&L). New-sales contribution = $127.8M × 30% × 20% = $7.7M. Net −$10.4M.
Fee reset
Delivered 703k, click-and-collect 637k. Cost $7.40 × 1,340k + ($13.80 − $6.40) × 703k = $15.1M. Saving $3.0M − $0.5M (2% of sales × 20%) − $0.3M (3% rate rise) = $2.2M.
Stores
$3.1M loss removed + $118M × 25% × 12% = $3.5M → $6.6M for nine; × 6/9 = $4.4M; × 3/9 = $2.2M vs $7.5M exit cost.
Promotions and vendors

3 pts × 14 pts × $1,503M = $6.3M. The 14-pt gap is read as net of vendor funding: gross markdown ≈ 14 ÷ (1 − 46%) = 25.9 pts on promotional sales; 1 point of funding ≈ 25.9% × 26% × $1,503M × 1% ≈ $1.0M.
Other
Shrink 0.3 pts × $1,503M = $4.5M. Private label 2 pts × 12 pts × $1,503M = $3.6M. Labor 3% × ~$172M (after exits) = $5.2M.
Source: Harlow briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data); team analysis.

slides.title: Appendix: assumptions and judgment calls made in preparing this deck

paragraphs.text: APPENDIX
Appendix: assumptions and judgment calls made in preparing this deck
Plan year
Follows the briefing pack: FY2026 is the first plan year and the covenant test year. If FY2026 has already largely run its course, the first-90-day actions matter most for FY2027.
Scale

Levers are sized as annual run-rates at FY2025 scale, with no underlying drift. If promotional creep and e-commerce growth continued at the FY2024–25 pace, operating income would keep falling by ~$15–18M a year, which is why the first wave is urgent.
Lost e-commerce sales
All sales lost from the fee change are treated as new-to-Harlow (the conservative case); some will shift to stores.
Store split
The pack gives only totals for the nine stores; benefits are split pro rata. No one-time cost is in the pack for the six lease-end exits; it is covered by the $10M allowance.
Implementation budget
$10M one-time allowance for closures, shrink controls, private-label development and promotion analytics is our estimate; the pack does not provide these costs.
Promotion and private-label targets
Promotional share of ~26% (FY2024 level) and private label of 20.5% (continuing the FY2023–25 trend) are management choices to validate, not forecasts.
Team claims
The e-commerce 6.1% margin and "promotions work" claims are recomputed or qualified using finance’s data, as shown on pages 4 and 6.
Source: Harlow briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data); team analysis.
